title: Every step was downhill. Why did the path zigzag?
usage: Reviewed exam-eve scenario content. Plain-text explanations only; the concept sketch is hand-authored static SVG rendered from the description below. Scenario choices are page state and never modify coverage, pins, priority, or exported notebook data.

scenarios.heading: Scenario A · The zigzag
scenarios.setup: You are running steepest descent with exact line searches in a long, narrow valley. Each new direction is perpendicular to the last, so you keep re-stepping in nearly the same directions and bounce across the valley walls. Progress toward the far end is painfully slow.

choices.label: Use a bigger learning rate
choices.reveal: A longer step along the same steep directions just throws you farther across the valley. The directions are the problem, not their length.

choices.label: Randomize the directions
choices.reveal: Random directions carry no memory of earlier progress and no guarantee of pointing downhill. CG chooses each direction deliberately from the previous ones.

choices.label: Use A-orthogonal (conjugate) directions
choices.reveal: For two different directions p and q, p-transpose A q equals zero, so the directions are decoupled in the geometry of the quadratic. Progress made along one direction is never undone by the next step, so the zigzag disappears.

visual.label: Concept sketch
visual.description: A hand-authored, qualitative narrow elliptical valley with the minimum marked at its centre. A dashed polyline labelled "Steepest descent" zigzags across the valley, bouncing between the walls and creeping toward the centre. A solid path labelled "Conjugate gradient" reaches the centre in two conjugate moves, each along a different axis of the ellipse. Diagram labels stay readable as text on mobile; dashed versus solid lines carry the distinction as well as colour.
visual.screenReaderSummary: Concept sketch: in a narrow elliptical valley, a dashed steepest-descent zigzag bounces across the walls while a solid conjugate-gradient path reaches the centre in two moves.

scenarios.heading: Scenario B · Why A-orthogonality?
scenarios.setup: In exact arithmetic, CG solves an n-dimensional quadratic in at most n steps. Each direction is finished for good once you minimize along it.
scenarios.prompt: Which inner product defines conjugacy here?

choices.label: The standard dot product.
choices.reveal: Ordinary orthogonality between successive steps is what steepest descent already gives you, and it is what produces the zigzag. It ignores the curvature that A encodes.

choices.label: The matrix-weighted inner product ⟨p, Aq⟩.
choices.reveal: Conjugacy means ⟨p, Aq⟩ equals zero for different directions, which is orthogonality in the geometry of the symmetric positive-definite matrix A. Under that inner product, minimizing along one direction leaves progress along the others intact.

scenarios.takeaway: Conjugate directions decouple the problem — each step finishes one direction for good.
